notes:
I've written notes for verses 1, 6, 8, 15 and 20 only. My research tools stopped working partway through, so verses 2–5, 7, 9–14, 16–19 and 21 have nothing yet. You asked me to leave out what I couldn't find, so they're missing rather than filled in from memory. Next to read: Bible Hub's commentary pages for each verse, Guzik/Enduring Word, and the GotQuestions pages on verses 5 and 7 (I saw they exist but didn't read them).

---

**v. 1: "servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God"**

- **Word studies (older commentaries):** One older note says the Greek word for "servants" originally meant rowers at the oar, which shows how hard a faithful minister works. The original word, υπηρετας, properly signifies such servants as laboured at the oar in rowing vessels. Another adds that a steward in a Greek household was usually a slave, but one given great trust. Though servants, their office is one of great trust... It is to be remembered that even the steward in a Greek household was generally a slave. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/4-1.htm
- **Barnes:** Calling ministers "stewards" lifts up the leaders Paul seemed to play down in 3:5. "Mysteries" are gospel truths that were hidden until Christ revealed them. The apostle by using the term here seems to have designed to elevate those whom he seemed to have depreciated in 1 Corinthians 3:5. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/4-1.htm
- **Gill:** Ministers are not masters of God's house who can do as they please. They are its highest officers, given God's hidden things to hand out, such as the Trinity and the incarnation. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rhe/1-corinthians/4-1.html
- **Where Protestants differ: does "mysteries" include the sacraments?**
  - *Reformed (Ligonier):* Yes. This is a ministry God calls men to, and it covers baptism and the Lord's Supper. When Paul refers to "stewards of the mysteries of God," the church understands that to include being "stewards of the sacraments." https://learn.ligonier.org/qas/who-can-administer-the-sacraments
  - *Matthew Poole (Puritan):* Also yes. Ministers are stewards of Christ's teachings and institutions, which we usually comprehend under the terms of the word and sacraments. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/4-1.htm
  - *Baptist (John MacArthur, gty.org):* MacArthur defines a mystery as revealed truth, not anything mystical: a truth that was previously hidden but is now widely known by divine revelation and apostolic proclamation. The apostles declared these truths openly, and they now stand written in the New Testament. https://www.gty.org/articles/A319/true-servants-of-christ
  - *Adam Clarke (Methodist):* Clarke reads the mysteries as God's teachings about salvation through Christ's death and the Spirit's work in the soul. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rhe/1-corinthians/4-1.html
  - *An older note (unnamed on the page):* It warns against reading "sacraments" back into Paul. In later patristic usage the word means "sacraments;" but St. Paul has expressly said (1 Corinthians 1:17) that his mission was to preach the gospel, not primarily to administer the sacraments. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/4-1.htm

**v. 6: "not to go beyond what is written"**

- **Calvin:** "What is written" could mean Paul's own writing or the Scripture passages he has already quoted. Calvin thinks the choice matters little and leaves it to the reader. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/4-6.html
- **Ellicott (as given on Bible Hub):** It doesn't point to one verse. It points to the general drift of the Old Testament, which always gives glory to God alone (see 1:19, 1:31, 3:19). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/4-6.htm
- **The text and the "proverb" view:** Older notes say the best manuscripts leave out the word "think." They read the phrase as a short saying, like "nothing too much," whose exact meaning is uncertain. The word "to think" is omitted in the best manuscripts. The phrase, "which have been written," is of very uncertain meaning. Vincent also calls it a proverbial expression. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/4-6.htm
- **Barnes:** Paul probably means what he wrote in 3:5–9, 3:21 and 4:1, or Scripture's general call to humility. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/4-6.html
- **Matthew Henry:** The cure for church factions is to think modestly of ourselves and not rate our teachers above what Scripture says about them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/4-6.html
- **Constable:** Going beyond what God has written means going beyond Scripture's teaching. Avoiding that keeps people from boasting in one teacher over another. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/4-6.html
- **Guzik:** Guzik warns that people now call something "biblical" just because no verse condemns it, and that is exactly thinking beyond what is written. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/1-corinthians/1-corinthians-4.cfm
- **GotQuestions:** Nobody is sure where the saying came from, but the Corinthians clearly knew it. The site reads it as a statement that Scripture is enough and that truth doesn't depend on a teacher's charisma. https://www.gotquestions.org/not-go-beyond-what-is-written.html
- **A stricter reading (Churches of Christ writers on StudyLight):**
  - *Coffman* holds that the traditional reading, that Christians must order their service of God by Scripture alone, is without any doubt whatever the true interpretation.
  - *"Living By Faith"* applies the verse to church work, worship and structure. For example, a church headquarters the New Testament doesn't describe goes beyond what is written. It also rejects the "proverb" reading.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/4-6.html
- **Bible Hub topical article:** It ties the verse to Reformation sola scriptura. It also argues that creeds and tradition are acceptable only when they come from Scripture and submit to it. https://biblehub.com/q/what_does_'not_go_beyond'_mean.htm

**v. 8: "Already you have become rich… kings"**

- **Constable:** The Corinthians acted as if they had already been rewarded at Christ's judgment seat, an indication of their over-realized eschatology. In other words, they thought the future reign had already arrived. Paul's wish is ironic: he would be glad if reward-time had really come so he could reign with them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/4-8.html
- **Bible Hub commentaries (Jamieson-Fausset-Brown wording, though the page doesn't name it):** The stress falls on "already" and "without us." The Corinthians acted as if they no longer needed to hunger for righteousness. The note adds that real wealth at Corinth probably fed this spiritual self-satisfaction, set against Paul's literal hunger in v. 11. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/4-8.htm
- **Poole and Gill:** Poole says they thought themselves so full of knowledge that they needed no more teaching. Gill compares them to the Laodiceans (Rev. 3:17), who thought they were rich but were poor. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/4-8.htm
- **Bible Hub study notes:** The verse shows a misunderstanding of God's kingdom, which is not yet fully here on earth. https://biblehub.com/study/1_corinthians/4-8.htm
- I found no source on these sites that applies v. 8 to prosperity or word-of-faith teaching, so I've left that out.

**v. 15: "in Christ Jesus I became your father"**

- **Catholic reading (catholic.com):** Catholics use this verse to answer the charge that Matthew 23:9 forbids calling priests "Father." If St. Paul does this, then the Church is on solid ground in calling her priests "father." https://www.catholic.com/bible-navigator/calling-priests-father/1corinthians414-15,17. Another catholic.com article says other fathers, physical or spiritual, share in God's one fatherhood without taking it over. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/fatherly-wisdom
- **Protestant replies (as reported by catholic.com):**
  - Paul was describing a real relationship, since he led them to faith, not claiming a church title.
  - Paul uses a verb, "begot," not the noun "father" for himself.
  - The article answers that Paul's contrast with "many fathers" implies he *is* their father.
  - https://www.catholic.com/magazine/blog/protestants-fight-back-on-call-no-man-father
- **Evangelical view (GotQuestions):** It notes that nowhere are any of the apostles addressed as "father" by other believers. It quotes MacArthur that in Matthew 23 Jesus condemns pride and pretense, not titles as such. https://www.gotquestions.org/spiritual-father.html

**v. 20: "not a matter of talk but of power"**

- **Calvin:** "The kingdom of God" here means how the gospel is run, through which God rules his church. Smooth teaching without power is like a beautiful body with no soul. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/4-20.html
- **Matthew Henry:** The kingdom spreads not by clever argument but by the Spirit's power: in miraculous operations at first, and the powerful influence of divine truth on the minds and manners of men. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/4-20.html
- **Adam Clarke (Methodist):** The power is the Holy Spirit's mighty energy enlightening, converting and sanctifying believers. Clarke adds that true apostles could prove their calling by miracles when needed, which the Greek word often means. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nkj/1-corinthians/4-20.html
- **Poole:** In each person, the kingdom shows up in the power God's word has to overcome sinful desires. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/4-20.html
- **Constable:** Paul is coming back to his words-versus-power contrast from 2:1–5. Real power is the Spirit working through humble messengers. "Kingdom" here includes God's rule over the church now, not only the future kingdom. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/4-20.html
- **A charismatic-style reading (Light of Israel Bible Commentary):** It links "power" to preaching where people are saved, healed and delivered. It points to "power encounters" on mission fields, with demons bound and healing miracles. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/4-20.html
- **A warning against taking "not in word" too far ("Living By Faith"):** Read literally, the phrase would mean the church does no teaching. The writer takes it to mean "not *only* in word": the kingdom involves both word and power. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/4-20.html

**Gaps:** I didn't reach the Pentecostal, Lutheran, Wesleyan-specific, Orthodox or modern-scholarship sites you listed (such as ag.org, lcms.org, oca.org, netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org).
